title: The Westphalian Order and Early Constitutionalism

slides.title: The Westphalian Order of International Law and the Emergence of the Modern State
slides.text: Lena Foljanty, 29 October 2025.

slides.title: The thread of the unit
slides.text: Legislation in the territories and municipalities increases from the late Middle Ages, and out of that grows the early modern state. Five steps, and the lecture follows them in order: the increasing influence of Roman law; POLICEY ORDINANCES as a new form of legislation on every level — towns, territories, Empire; the idea of SOVEREIGNTY arising in the religious wars of the 17th century; the development of IUS PUBLICUM; and the emergence of a unitary state in the age of absolutism.

cards.q: Name the five steps by which the early modern state emerges, in order.
cards.a: Increasing influence of Roman law; Policey ordinances as a new form of legislation at town, territorial and imperial level; the idea of sovereignty arising out of the religious wars of the 17th century; the development of ius publicum as a discipline; and the emergence of a unitary state under absolutism.

slides.title: The Reformation as the fundamental shift
slides.text: The 16th-century split of the church into Protestantism and Catholicism was FUNDAMENTAL for the development of the Empire. Luther nailed his 95 theses at Wittenberg in 1517, and everything that follows in this unit — the wars, the peace, the idea of sovereignty, public law as a discipline — grows out of a religious division that the existing legal order had no way to absorb.

slides.title: The legal consequences of the split
slides.text: Two things follow, and the second is the interesting one. First, an INTENSIFICATION OF REGIONAL RULE: Protestant princes secure suzerainty over the regional church, so the prince gains a whole new domain of authority. Second, entirely new legal problems demanding new solutions — the appropriation of CHURCH PROPERTY for municipal and sovereign purposes, and conflicts arising from religious differences between imperial estates and inside the imperial bodies themselves. And where are the solutions sought? IN THE LEGISLATION OF THE EMPIRE. The religious split is what drives the Empire to legislate.

cards.q: Which new legal problems did the religious split create, and where were solutions sought?
cards.a: The appropriation of church property for municipal and sovereign purposes, and conflicts from religious differences between the imperial estates and within the imperial bodies. Solutions were sought in the legislation of the Empire — the split is what drove the Empire to legislate.

cards.q: How did the Reformation strengthen the territorial princes?
cards.a: Protestant princes secured suzerainty over the regional church, which intensified regional rule and handed the prince a new domain of authority.

slides.title: The religious wars
slides.text: The 16th and 17th centuries bring numerous religious wars: peasant wars, Protestant estates against the Emperor, and claims of religious freedom and in part of PERSONAL freedom. There are repeated attempts to regulate the conflict LEGALLY — the PEACE OF AUGSBURG of 1555 above all. And yet the wars continue: civil war in France and wars between Protestant estates and the Emperor in the second half of the 16th century, and then the THIRTY YEARS' WAR, 1618–1648. Augsburg is the attempt; the Thirty Years' War is the measure of how far it fell short.

terms.def: The first legal settlement of the religious conflict in the Empire, source of 'cuius regio, eius religio'. Confirmed and extended at Westphalia.

cards.q: Which legal attempt was made to settle the religious conflict, and what shows it was not enough?
cards.a: The Peace of Augsburg of 1555. That it was not enough is shown by what followed: civil war in France, wars between Protestant estates and the Emperor in the later 16th century, and the Thirty Years' War of 1618–1648.

slides.title: The Battle of White Mountain
slides.text: Peter Snayers' painting of the battle of 1620, the opening phase of the Thirty Years' War — and, for the Bohemian lands, the end of the estates' power.

slides.title: The Peace of Westphalia, 1648
slides.text: The Thirty Years' War had devastated the country with severe population loss. It ends in 1648 with the Peace of Münster and the TREATIES OF OSNABRÜCK AND MÜNSTER — adopted as part of the LEGES FUNDAMENTALES in 1654, which is what makes them constitutional law of the Empire and not merely a peace treaty. And the settlement does two distinct things, which the exam expects to be kept apart: it RE-ORDERS EUROPE, and it RE-ORDERS THE EMPIRE.

terms.def: The fundamental laws of the Empire. The Westphalian treaties were adopted among them in 1654, turning a peace settlement into constitutional law.

cards.q: What exactly is the Peace of Westphalia, and what made it constitutional law?
cards.a: The Peace of Münster and the Treaties of Osnabrück and Münster, 1648, ending the Thirty Years' War. They became constitutional law of the Empire by being adopted among the leges fundamentales in 1654.

cards.q: The Peace of Westphalia does two separate things. Which?
cards.a: It re-orders EUROPE — the map and the balance of powers — and it re-orders THE EMPIRE — its internal constitution. Keep the two apart.

slides.title: Re-ordering Europe
slides.text: Switzerland and the Northern Netherlands LEAVE the Empire. Spanish power is diminished — Portugal and the Northern Netherlands had become independent of Spain in 1640. And FRANCE and SWEDEN become important powers. The European balance that the next century and a half runs on is set here.

cards.q: What did the Peace of Westphalia change on the European map?
cards.a: Switzerland and the Northern Netherlands left the Empire; Spanish power was diminished, Portugal and the Northern Netherlands having become independent of Spain in 1640; and France and Sweden rose to become important powers.

slides.title: Re-ordering the Empire
slides.text: Four changes, and together they are a far-reaching constitutional reform. EQUAL RECOGNITION of the three confessions — Catholic, Lutheran, Calvinist — confirming the Augsburg rule CUIUS REGIO, EIUS RELIGIO, fixed to the state of things in 1624. LIMITATION OF THE EMPEROR'S POWER: the fundamental competences — legislation, declaration of war and peace, the right of alliance, and supreme jurisdiction — are bound to the CONSENT OF THE REICHSTAG. Separation of the imperial estates into CONFESSIONAL CORPS, which makes the imperial constitution even more complicated. And SOVEREIGNTY to the imperial princes over their territories. Note the direction: the Empire does not become a state, it becomes a framework inside which its members do.

terms.def: 'Whose realm, his religion' — the ruler's confession determines the territory's. From Augsburg 1555, confirmed at Westphalia with the state of 1624 as the reference year.

cards.q: Which competences of the Emperor were bound to the consent of the Reichstag in 1648?
cards.a: Legislation, declaration of war and peace, the right of alliance, and supreme jurisdiction — the fundamental competences. That is the constitutional core of the settlement.

cards.q: What does 'cuius regio, eius religio' mean, where does it come from, and what reference year did Westphalia fix?
cards.a: 'Whose realm, his religion' — the ruler's confession determines that of his territory. It comes from the Peace of Augsburg of 1555; Westphalia confirmed it and fixed the state of things as of 1624, now with equal recognition of Catholic, Lutheran and Calvinist.

cards.q: In which direction did Westphalia move power inside the Empire?
cards.a: Downwards. The Emperor's competences were tied to the Reichstag's consent and the imperial princes gained sovereignty over their territories — the Empire became a framework within which its members became states.

slides.title: Source: Article VIII of the Peace of Osnabrück
slides.text: § 1 — so that no disputes shall arise in future in the political order, every Elector, Prince and Estate of the Roman Empire shall be so fortified in their ancient rights, advantages, liberty, privileges and THE FREE EXERCISE OF THE SOVEREIGNTY OF THE LAND that they may never be physically disturbed by anyone under any pretext. § 2 — above all, the RIGHT TO CONCLUDE ALLIANCES among themselves and with FOREIGN countries for their preservation and security shall always be free to the individual estates — ON CONDITION that such alliances are not directed against the Emperor and the Empire and its peace, or against this treaty, and that the oath binding each to the Emperor and the Empire remains inviolate. Read the two paragraphs together and you have the whole ambiguity of the settlement: a right to make foreign alliances, coupled with a continuing oath of allegiance. Sovereign, and still a member.

cards.q: What does Article VIII of the Peace of Osnabrück grant the imperial estates, and under what condition?
cards.a: § 1 fortifies their ancient rights and the free exercise of the sovereignty of the land, so that they may never be disturbed under any pretext. § 2 grants the right to conclude alliances among themselves and with foreign powers for their preservation and security — on condition that the alliances are not directed against the Emperor, the Empire, its peace or the treaty, and that the oath binding each to the Emperor remains inviolate.

cards.q: Why is Article VIII of Osnabrück the ambiguity of Westphalia in miniature?
cards.a: Because it gives the estates a right to make alliances with foreign powers — an attribute of sovereignty — while keeping their oath to the Emperor inviolate and forbidding alliances against the Empire. They are sovereign and still members at the same time.

slides.title: The same article in German
slides.text: The German wording of Article VIII of the Peace of Osnabrück, with the key phrase 'die freie Ausübung der Landeshoheit' — the free exercise of territorial sovereignty.

slides.title: Westphalia and international law
slides.text: The Peace of Westphalia is WIDELY SEEN as the beginning of modern international relations — note the hedge, because it is a claim about how later ages read it as much as about 1648 itself. Three grounds are given: it is the first attempt to CODIFY international law; it sets new STANDARDS for peace negotiations as to actors, mediation, documentation and diplomacy; and the idea of TERRITORIAL SOVEREIGNTY emerges — even if there were still certain limits, as Article VIII shows.

cards.q: On what grounds is Westphalia called the beginning of modern international relations, and what qualification does the lecture add?
cards.a: It is the first attempt to codify international law, it sets new standards for peace negotiations (actors, mediation, documentation, diplomacy), and it brings the idea of territorial sovereignty. The qualification: it is 'widely seen' that way, and the sovereignty it granted still had limits.

slides.title: Bodin and the idea of sovereignty
slides.text: The idea goes back to JEAN BODIN, Les six livres de la république, 1576. Its context is the religious CIVIL WAR IN FRANCE, and Bodin argues on two fronts at once: against the PROTESTANT claim that the monarch's authority should be limited, and against MACHIAVELLI's Il principe (1513) and its claim that the monarch may rule CONTRA LEGEM when the state requires it. The book is then intensely studied in the EMPIRE, where the relation between Emperor and estates had been under negotiation since the Reformation: how far do the legal means of the Catholic Emperor reach against Protestant imperial estates? Out of that, the question that defines sovereignty ever since — WHO DECIDES.

terms.def: Les six livres de la république (1576), written in the French religious civil war. Founds the modern concept of sovereignty, against Protestant limits on the monarch and against Machiavelli's rule contra legem.

cards.q: Against whom does Bodin argue in Les six livres de la république, and on which two fronts?
cards.a: Against the Protestant claim that the monarch's authority should be limited, and against Machiavelli's Il principe (1513), which held that the monarch may rule contra legem for the sake of the state. Bodin's context is the French religious civil war of 1576.

cards.q: Why was Bodin studied so intensely in the Empire?
cards.a: Because since the Reformation the relation between Emperor and estates had been under negotiation — how far the legal means of the Catholic Emperor reached against Protestant imperial estates. That made the question 'who decides' the central one, which is exactly what sovereignty answers.

slides.title: Source: Bodin on the sovereign and the law
slides.text: If the sovereign Prince is exempt from the laws of his predecessors, much less is he bound by the laws he makes himself — for one may receive law from others, but IT IS IMPOSSIBLE BY NATURE TO GIVE ONESELF LAW, or to command oneself in a thing that depends on one's own will. Hence the closing formula of edicts and ordinances: FOR SUCH IS OUR PLEASURE — making clear that the laws of the sovereign Prince, though founded on good and strong reasons, depend ONLY on his pure and frank will. But as to the DIVINE AND NATURAL laws, all the Princes of the earth are subject to them and it is not in their power to contravene them. Two halves, and both are examined: the sovereign is above his own law, and below divine and natural law.

cards.q: Bodin: why is the sovereign not bound by his own laws?
cards.a: Because it is impossible by nature to give oneself law, or to command oneself in something that depends on one's own will. One may receive law from another, but not from oneself — hence the formula closing edicts, 'for such is our pleasure'.

cards.q: Is Bodin's sovereign subject to any law at all?
cards.a: Yes — to divine and natural law. All the princes of the earth are subject to those and it is not in their power to contravene them. Sovereignty is freedom from positive law, not from every law.

slides.title: The same passage in French
slides.text: Bodin's text in the original, with the formula 'CAR TEL EST NOTRE PLAISIR'.

slides.title: Absolutism
slides.text: The definition to learn: ABSOLUTISM is a concept of rule in which the monarch rules WITHOUT THE ESTATES — supreme legislator, supreme judge and supreme official IN ONE PERSON. It is legitimized by the work of philosophers and jurists, Bodin and Hobbes among them, and established in the larger countries of the Empire and in France. Two concrete markers: in the HABSBURG MONARCHY the disempowerment of the estates begins with the Renewed Land Code for Bohemia and Moravia, 1627/28 — that is, straight after White Mountain; in FRANCE the Estates General are not convoked AT ALL between 1614 and 1789. The French date is worth holding: the gap ends where the Revolution begins.

terms.def: Rule in which the monarch governs without the estates, uniting supreme legislator, supreme judge and supreme official in one person.
Verneuerte Landesordnung for Bohemia and Moravia — the beginning of the disempowerment of the estates in the Habsburg Monarchy, following the Battle of White Mountain.

cards.q: Define absolutism and name its three offices.
cards.a: A concept of rule in which the monarch rules without the estates, uniting in one person the supreme legislator, the supreme judge and the supreme official.

cards.q: Give one concrete marker of absolutism in the Habsburg Monarchy and one in France.
cards.a: Habsburg: the Renewed Land Code for Bohemia and Moravia of 1627/28, which begins the disempowerment of the estates after White Mountain. France: the Estates General are not convoked between 1614 and 1789 — the gap ends with the Revolution.

slides.title: Enlightened absolutism in Austria
slides.text: The age of reforms under Maria Theresa and Joseph II — enlightened, but PATERNALISTIC. The two formulas say it exactly: the monarch as 'the first servant of the state', and 'EVERYTHING FOR THE PEOPLE, NOTHING BY THE PEOPLE'. Personal and religious freedom are strengthened: legislation on the status of subjects and the ABOLITION OF SERVITUDE in 1781, and in the same year the right of confessional minorities to practise their faith PRIVATELY. Note both limits — privately, and nothing BY the people.

terms.def: Absolute rule exercised for the good of the subjects on rational principles — 'everything for the people, nothing by the people'. The monarch as first servant of the state.

cards.q: What do the two formulas of enlightened absolutism mean?
cards.a: 'The first servant of the state' — the monarch justifies his rule by service rather than by person — and 'everything for the people, nothing by the people' — reforms are made FOR the subjects, but they get no share in making them. Enlightened, and paternalistic.

cards.q: Which two freedoms were strengthened in Austria in 1781, and what limited each?
cards.a: The status of subjects, with the abolition of servitude; and the right of confessional minorities to practise their faith — but only PRIVATELY. Both are grants from above, in keeping with 'nothing by the people'.

slides.title: Building the unitary state
slides.text: Two achievements. THE UNITARY STATE: the estates are largely disempowered — but NEVER COMPLETELY ABOLISHED — centralized bureaucratic structures are set up, and a police in the modern sense is established. And the SEPARATION OF JUSTICE AND ADMINISTRATION: the Habsburg Monarchy creates a Supreme Judicial Office (Oberste Justizstelle) and Courts of Appeal, while Frederick II of Prussia PROMISES non-interference in judicial decisions. Notice how the independence of the judiciary begins — as a promise by an absolute monarch, not as a right against him.

cards.q: How was justice separated from administration under enlightened absolutism?
cards.a: In the Habsburg Monarchy by creating a Supreme Judicial Office (Oberste Justizstelle) and Courts of Appeal; in Prussia by Frederick II's promise not to interfere in judicial decisions. Judicial independence begins as a monarch's promise, not as a right against him.

cards.q: What is meant by the creation of a unitary state, and what was NOT done?
cards.a: The estates were largely disempowered, centralized bureaucratic structures were built and a police in the modern sense established. What was not done: the estates were never completely abolished.

slides.title: Ius publicum becomes a discipline
slides.text: Three pressures produce a new academic subject. Increasing LOCAL legislation from the 15th century — Policey ordinances, land and municipal law reformations. Reforms at the level of the EMPIRE — the reforms of 1495, the regulations arising from religious conflict 1519–1555, the reform of the Emperor's election in 1519, the imperial Policey ordinances of 1530, 1548 and 1577. And the CONFLICTS from the religious schism — over ecclesiastical property, and over religious differences within the estates and the imperial organs. Out of these, debates on the fundamental questions of the CONSTITUTIO of the Empire arise at the universities, and from the 17th century PUBLIC LAW develops as a discipline of its own. Public law is born out of an argument nobody could settle.

terms.def: Public law as a distinct academic discipline, emerging from the 17th century out of the unresolved constitutional disputes of the Empire.

cards.q: What produced public law as a distinct discipline, and when?
cards.a: From the 17th century, out of three pressures: increasing local legislation (Policey ordinances, land and municipal reformations) from the 15th century, reforms at imperial level (1495, 1519–1555, the imperial Policey ordinances of 1530, 1548, 1577), and the conflicts of the religious schism. The resulting debates on the constitution of the Empire moved into the universities.

slides.title: Summary of the unit
slides.text: The religious conflicts of the 16th and 17th centuries become the PROPELLER of modern statehood. The Peace of Westphalia of 1648 re-orders both the Empire and international law; out of it comes the modern idea of SOVEREIGNTY, which is the ground on which the idea of ABSOLUTIST rule is built; and the idea of a RATIONAL state leads on to enlightened absolutism in the 18th century. Public law emerging as a discipline from the 17th century accompanies the whole process. The chain to remember: religious war → sovereignty → absolutism → enlightened absolutism, with public law as its commentary.

cards.q: Give the chain of this unit in one line.
cards.a: Religious conflict in the 16th–17th centuries → the Peace of Westphalia (1648) re-orders the Empire and international law → the modern idea of sovereignty → absolutism → the idea of a rational state → enlightened absolutism in the 18th century, with public law emerging as a discipline alongside from the 17th century.
